extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and news reporters (writers of newspaper weather and related local-interest stories)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and writing newspaper weather pieces and related local-interest items (storms, seasonal changes, eclipses), showing what subjects to cover, how to angle them, and stylistic approaches from straight informative to colorful human-interest treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence of official forecasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Official forecasts of the weather are given a place of prominence on the front page of most papers, and are read with interest by most readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place official forecasts prominently (front page placement is common). Use the Weather Bureau's forecast as a key element of coverage because readers rely on it for planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitable subjects for weather stories
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of the seasons, extremes of heat and cold, storms, and unusual weather of any sort serve as subjects for weather stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a range of meteorological events as story subjects; the author also notes inclusion of eclipses (though 'such phenomena should be classed as astronomical rather than meteorological'), so determine beat/classification appropriately when topics border disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of tone: informative vs lighter/humorous
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the purely informative type of story is the usual one for weather, the subject may be treated in a lighter vein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may write strictly informative accounts or adopt a lighter, humorous, or colorful treatment. Either approach can be appropriate — aim to add life and color regardless of whether the piece is mainly factual or entertaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize practical effects on readers (health, business, pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The universal interest in the weather... is due to its effect upon health, business, and pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Angle stories to show direct impacts on the audience — farmers, business people, shoppers, pleasure-seekers — so the reader understands why the weather matters in practical terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide concrete local impacts and specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Report effects on local commerce, transport, services, and daily life (examples: coastal shipping paralyzed, rail traffic halted, trolley lines affected, stores closing early, telephone company rush).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise local details — streets, businesses, transit lines, institutions — and quantify operational disruptions (delays, closures, extra service) to show the real-world consequences of weather.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise measurements and historical/contextual data
rubrics_metrics.description: Give specific temperature readings, forecasts, comparisons to normals, and historical record comparisons (e.g., exact thermometric readings, accumulated excesses of heat, dates and depths of past snowfalls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include numeric data (temperatures, times, inches of snow) and historical context (records and past events) to situate today's weather relative to norms and past extremes; when covering astronomical events, include precise times of contact and observational measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain meteorological causes and future expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute conditions to larger systems (example: area of high barometric pressure moving eastward causing cold), and forecast likely near-term developments (e.g., risk of frost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, explain why the weather is occurring (pressure systems, winds) and what to expect next, so readers can prepare (protect crops, anticipate travel disruption). Include expert/forecaster interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include vivid human anecdotes and scene details
rubrics_metrics.description: There is often a chance for life and color whether the treatment be informative or more or less humorous; stories include anecdotes (people slipping, rescuing, carrying babes, a man’s Easter hat blown away) to enliven the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add short human-interest vignettes and colorful descriptive detail to make the story engaging and relatable — scenes of people, animals, merchants, or entertainers reacting to the weather help the reader connect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote officials, experts, and participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotations from forecasters, municipal officials, business agents, union leaders, and witnesses (examples: forecaster Smith; Rollin A. Keyes; Alex Gilchrist; Prof. W.S. Eichelberger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute statements to named sources (officials, experts, participants) to lend authority and perspective; include explanatory comments from them about causes, impacts, or future actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report casualties, damage, and official response for severe events
rubrics_metrics.description: In storms and disasters include counts of dead, wounded, missing, property damage, and descriptions of rescue and relief actions (e.g., militia action, fires set, tents burned, rescue by Red Cross, troops’ movements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For violent or damaging weather-related events, document human toll and property loss, sequence of events, and official/organizational responses; be precise and cautious with figures (use 'known tonight' phrasing when counts are provisional).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify phenomena to the proper beat (meteorology vs astronomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two stories of an eclipse are included in the weather division, although, of course, such phenomena should be classed as astronomical rather than meteorological.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of subject boundaries and classify/route coverage appropriately; treat eclipses with scientific precision but recognize they fall under astronomy rather than routine weather reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present alternative reporting styles for the same facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes — In the next two stories the facts about the same eclipse are given in different ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to present the same factual material in a straightforward factual manner or a more literary, playful, or descriptive style; both are acceptable and illustrate how tone and presentation change the reader's experience.
